Acknowledgements
This report was researched and written by Nick Cumming-Bruce, 
Rula Daoud, Laurène Deglaire, Alex Frost, Emil Hasanov, Lucy 
Pinches, Frances Smith, and Louise Wilson. The Mine Action Review 
project is managed by Lucy Pinches. The report was edited by 
Stuart Casey-Maslen and laid out by Optima Design in the United 
Kingdom. Mine Action Review would like to thank Global Affairs 
Canada, the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the 
Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation (NORAD), and  
the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs for funding its 
work. We would also like to thank all those who contributed data 
and information, including national mine action authorities and 
mine action centres, clearance operators, UN agencies, and other  
expert mine action organisations.

The report and the views expressed in it are the work of the 
authors. The designation of armed non-state actors, states, or 
territories does not imply any judgement by Norwegian People’s 
Aid (NPA), Global Affairs Canada, the French Ministry for Europe 
and Foreign Affairs, the Norwegian Agency for Development 
Cooperation (NORAD), the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign 
Affairs or any other organisation, body, or individual regarding 
the legal status of such actors, states, or territories, or their 
authorities and institutions, or the delimitation of their boundaries, 
or the status of any states or territories that border them.
Other information
Mine Action Review is an independent research project published by NPA.
This publication is available for download at www.mineactionreview.org
The report focuses on anti-personnel mine land release data for the calendar year 2024, with information  
on other aspects of survey and clearance programmes included up to November 2025 where possible.
Mine Action Review welcomes comments from national authorities and other relevant stakeholders.

1   Clearing the Mines 2025
KEY FINDINGS
 ■ In 2024, a global total of 175.39 square kilometres  
of mined area was cleared of anti-personnel (AP) mines, 
which represents a drop of just over one quarter on the 
2023 figure of 237.85km 2 (which was the highest annual 
clearance output ever recorded). 1
The decrease in global clearance was largely due to 
38% reduction in clearance of mined area in State Party 
Cambodia, which fell by almost 50km 2 (although it still 
undertook greater mine clearance than any other State  
by a significant margin). 
Approximately 93% of AP mined area cleared worldwide 
in 2024 occurred in States Parties to the Anti-Personnel 
Mine Ban Convention (APMBC). Four States Parties 
with the greatest annual clearance output—Afghanistan, 
Cambodia, Croatia, and Iraq—accounted for almost 81%  
of all mined area cleared globally in 2024.
 ■ Globally, 131,190 AP mines were destroyed in the course of 
2024 during land release and explosive ordnance disposal 
(EOD) spot tasks, in 28 States Parties, eight States not 
party, and two “other areas” 2. The total number of AP 
mines destroyed in 2024 was a 33% reduction on the 
195,416 AP mines destroyed the year before. 3 The greatest 
number of mines destroyed in 2024 in a single State was 
in Zimbabwe (31,672), followed by Thailand (17,600), and 
Sri Lanka (16,510).
 ■ One State Party, Oman, fulfilled its clearance obligations 
in 2024, ahead of its Article 5 deadline of 1 February 2025, 
becoming the 33rd State freed of AP mined areas since 
1997 when the Convention was adopted.
 ■ As at 1 November 2025, globally 57 States (including 35 
States Parties) and 2 other areas were contaminated 
with AP mines. 4 This is one fewer than a year earlier, with 
State Party Oman removed from the global list following 
its completion of clearance. The Central African Republic  
(CAR) has also been taken off Mine Action Review’s list 
of affected State Parties pending further information, as 
hard evidence is lacking that areas containing improvised 
AP mines remain. In contrast, Algeria , which previously 
declared completion of Article 5 but which is finishing 
planned clearance of previously unknown mined areas, 
has been returned to Mine Action Review’s list of  
affected States. 
Algeria should seek a new Article 5 deadline while it 
completes this AP mine clearance. Cameroon  and Mali 
should also extend their already expired deadlines,  
as each has acknowledged new use of AP mines of  
an improvised nature on their respective territories  
by non-State armed groups (NSAGs) and therefore  
each has obligations under Article 5.
 ■ Based on Mine Action Review’s assessment of the extent 
of AP mine contamination  in affected States Parties, 
Afghanistan, Cambodia, Iraq , and Ukraine are massively 
contaminated (defined as covering more than 100km 2 
of land). Heavy contamination (covering more than 
20km2–100km2) exists in Angola, Bosnia and Herzegovina, 
Türkiye, and Yemen. In the other 27 affected States 
Parties, the extent of AP mine contamination is either 
medium or light. 
 ■ The extent of implementation of Article 5 clearance 
obligations varies widely between States Parties. Of the 
35 mine-affected States Parties as at 1 November 2025, 
only two were believed to be on track to meet their 
respective treaty deadlines – Croatia , which is just on 
track to meet its deadline of 1 March 2026; and Peru, 
which is on track to meet its recently extended deadline 
of 31 December 2029, having failed to meet its previous 
deadline of the end of 2024. 
 ■ Despite each having an obligation to implement Article 
5 “as soon as possible”, affected States Parties Türkiye 
and South Sudan each conducted less then 1km 2 of AP 
mine clearance in 2024; Algeria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, 
DR Congo, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Mauritania, Palestine, Peru, 
Senegal, Tajikistan, and Thailand each conducted less 
than 0.5km2 of AP mine clearance; and Burkina Faso, 
Cameroon, Chad, Cyprus, Eritrea, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, 
Niger, Nigeria, Serbia, and Sudan did not report any AP 
mine clearance at all for the year. Despite not releasing 
any mined area in 2024, Cameroon did, however, destroy 
10 AP mines during spot tasks; Chad destroyed 7 AP 
mines during route clearance; Guinea-Bissau released 
some mined area through technical survey (TS) and 
destroyed two AP mines; while Serbia released some 
mined area through TS. In contrast, Cyprus does not have 
effective control over remaining AP mined areas in the 
northern part of the island.

mineactionreview.org   2
 ■ Progress to complete Article 5 implementation in both 
Cambodia and neighbouring Thailand  is now contingent 
on the two States reaching agreement to clear the border 
minefields. The armed conflict between them in July 2025 
seems to have thwarted an early resolution of this critical 
issue. Cambodia has denied Thai accusations that it had 
newly emplaced AP mines, and the allegations remained 
unverified at the time of writing.
 ■ At the Fifth Review Conference of the APMBC, which took 
place in Siem Reap, Cambodia on 25–29 November 2024, 
States Parties adopted the five-year Siem Reap-Angkor 
Action Plan (SRAAP). The SRAAP is a blueprint for 
implementation of the Convention, supporting States 
Parties and their implementing partners get to completion 
in the best way possible – efficiently, effectively, safely, 
and inclusively. In addition to the official APMBC 
monitoring of the SRAAP, Mine Action Review is also 
providing civil society monitoring and analysis of the 
implementation of the SRAAP actions relating to survey 
and clearance . We encourage readers to refer to the 
separate report on the Mine Action Review website.
 ■ Of the non-signatories  for which clearance data was 
available, Azerbaijan conducted the most clearance  
of AP mined area in 2024, followed by Syria  and Israel.  
In Syria, the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 
has enabled a shift to a countrywide approach to mine 
action coordination, with operators reporting improved 
access and cooperation. However, major challenges 
remain, including a surge in casualties, persistent funding 
shortfalls, the absence of a national contamination 
baseline, only nascent managerial capacity in the 
transitional government, and ongoing security risks.  
Syria is reportedly considering acceding to the 
Convention, which is to be strongly encouraged.
 ■ Slow progress in clearance by affected States Parties 
and repeated Article 5 extension requests with little 
to no progress in between requests, should be of 
concern to the APMBC community. Of greatest concern 
at present, though, are the serious violations of the 
APMBC continue to be perpetrated by Ukraine – of its 
undertaking “never under any circumstances” to acquire, 
stockpile, and above all to use AP mines. These are grave 
threats to the integrity not only of the Convention but 
also to disarmament law more generally. What is more, 
Ukraine submitted an illegal declaration of suspension of 
implementation of its obligations in July 2025, to which 
several States Parties (notably Austria, Belgium, Norway, 
and Switzerland) had formally objected by the time of 
writing. Mine Action Review urges other States Parties 
to also formally object to Ukraine’s attempted unlawful 
suspension, and we call on Ukraine itself to rescind it. 
Five States Parties—Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, 
and Poland—have formally announced their withdrawal 
from the APMBC in the mistaken view that laying even 
millions of AP mines on their own territory will deter 
Russian aggression or, should the worst come to pass, 
stop or even just significantly delay an invasion. 
 ■ On top of these assaults on the universalisation 
and implementation of the Convention comes an 
unprecedented funding crisis , prompted by the decision 
by the United States to reconsider its hitherto staunch 
support to demining – first suspending its mine action 
funding to conduct a review and then reducing or 
terminating funding in many programmes. Furthermore, 
funding for mine action from other traditional donors, 
including European States, also appears to be at risk as 
States increase their defence spending, potentially at the 
expense of humanitarian and overseas aid budgets.

===PAGE 8===
3   Clearing the Mines 2025
OVERVIEW
SUMMARY OF CHALLENGES AND PROGRESS
The 1997 Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention (APMBC) is 
under pressure as never before in its 28-year history. Serious 
violations of core obligations, withdrawals by previously 
steadfast States Parties, use of improvised mines by armed 
groups, and a donor funding crisis are combining to create 
a perfect storm of headwinds. The most serious violations 
of the APMBC continue to be perpetrated by Ukraine – of its 
undertaking “never under any circumstances” to acquire, 
stockpile, and above all to use anti-personnel (AP) mines. 
These are grave threats to the integrity not only of the 
Convention but also to disarmament law more generally. 
What is more, Ukraine submitted an illegal declaration of 
suspension of implementation of its obligations in July 2025, 
which several States Parties (notably Austria, Belgium, 
Norway, and Switzerland) had formally objected to at the time 
of writing. Mine Action Review urges other States Parties to 
also formally object to the purported suspension and we call 
on Ukraine itself to rescind its unlawful action. Five States 
Parties—Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland—have 
formally announced their withdrawal from the APMBC in the 
mistaken view that laying and spraying even millions of AP 
mines on their own land will deter Russian aggression or, 
should the worst come to pass, stop or even just significantly 
delay an invasion. 
On top of these assaults on the universalisation and 
implementation of the Convention comes an unprecedented 
funding crisis, prompted by the decision by the United States 
to reconsider its hitherto staunch support to demining – first 
suspending its mine action funding to conduct a review and 
then reducing or terminating funding in many programmes. 
Furthermore, funding for mine action from other traditional 
donors, including European States, also appears to be at risk 
as States increase their defence spending, potentially at the 
expense of humanitarian and overseas aid budgets.
The impact of funding decisions of the US and other donor 
States on global mine clearance output will only start to 
impact in 2025 land release data and in the proceeding 
years, but already global output in 2024 was a 26% reduction 
compared to the previous year: down from almost 238 
square kilometres in 2023 to 175 square kilometres in 
2024. This was largely due to a massive drop in Cambodia 
in 2024, down nearly 50km 2 on the previous year due to a 
significant reduction in government funding for clearance 
compared to the previous year’s record high. Furthermore, 
Cambodia stands accused by Thailand of using AP mines, 
something which remained unverified at the time of writing. 
States Parties Afghanistan, Angola, and Iraq, together with 
non-signatory Azerbaijan, also recorded notable drops 
in clearance output in 2024, compared to 2023. A further 
drop in global clearance output in 2025 is to be expected. 
And although Finland has ruled out peacetime use of AP 
mines, the same is not true of the other four withdrawing 
States Parties, meaning the extent of mined areas may be 
aggravated instead of being tackled. We risk starting to move 
further away from the goal of a world free of AP mines.
There was, however, some light piercing through the dark 
shadows. At the end of 2024, Oman became the 33 rd State 
since the APMBC’s adoption to complete clearance; Oman 
reported having fulfilled its Article 5 obligations at the 
Convention’s Intersessional Meetings in Geneva in June 2025. 
At the time of writing, Croatia was (just) on track to become 
the 34th State freed of AP mined areas by its deadline of 1 
March 2026. It is similarly hoped that Algeria, which had 
prematurely declared Article 5 fulfilment in 2017 and which 
is currently without an extended Article 5 deadline, will 
complete planned clearance of all remaining mined areas 
before the Twenty-Third Meeting of States Parties in 2026. 
Somewhat attenuating the effect of the five withdrawals, in 
March 2025, the Marshall Islands ratified the Convention (its 
last remaining signatory State), while in June, Tonga acceded 
to it. They became the 165th and 166th States Parties to the 
APMBC, respectively. 
But if these positive developments are not to be the candle in 
the hurricane, all States Parties now need to show backbone 
and the President of the Twenty-Second Meeting of States 
Parties (22MSP), Ambassador Tomiko Ichikawa of Japan, 
must demonstrate genuine leadership. For the failure to 
confront serious violations of the Convention come December 
2025 will be paid for by the lives and limbs of innocent 
civilians around the world for years to come. Into the 
Ukrainian breach will surely go others who are confronted 
by an illegal use of force. At the Oslo Diplomatic Conference 
in 1997, the negotiating States grasped the nettle and stood 
up to the United States, which was trying to fundamentally 
weaken the putative treaty. The negotiating diplomats 
pledged in the very first preambular paragraph to “put an 
end to the suffering and casualties caused by anti-personnel 
mines, that kill or maim hundreds of people every week, 
mostly innocent and defenceless civilians and especially 
children, obstruct economic development and reconstruction, 
inhibit the repatriation of refugees and internally displaced 
persons, and have other severe consequences for years after 
emplacement”. Make it happen, States Parties.

mineactionreview.org   4
GLOBAL AP MINE CONTAMINATION: TWO STEPS FORWARD,  
ONE STEP BACK
As at 1 November 2025, globally 57 States and 2 “other 
areas”1 were contaminated by AP mines , as summarised 
in Table 1. While this headline figure is down by one from a 
year earlier, this masks a number of developments, some 
positive, some less so. Of the 57 affected States, 35 are party 
to the APMBC, one fewer than a year ago with Oman removed 
from the global list following its completion of clearance. 
The Central African Republic (CAR) has also been taken off 
Mine Action Review’s list of affected States pending further 
information, as hard evidence is lacking that areas containing 
improvised AP mines remain. In contrast, Algeria, with 
planned clearance of mined areas ongoing, has been returned 
to the list of affected States, its 2017 declaration of fulfilment 
of Article 5 proving to have been premature. 
At the time of writing, among the new total of 35 States 
Parties, four—Algeria, Burkina Faso , Cameroon , and 
Mali—did not have an Article 5 deadline in force. There is 
no suggestion of bad faith on Algeria’s part and importantly 
Algeria has been transparent in documenting its clearance 
and the number of AP mines destroyed in its annual Article 
7 reporting. But as occurred with Jordan more than a 
decade ago, Algeria has been steadily clearing mined areas 
it identified after its declaration of compliance while omitting 
to request a new clearance deadline as is expected in such 
a circumstance. Since declaring fulfilment of Article 5 on 10 
February 2017, Algeria cleared 30km 2 of mined area through 
to the end of 2024, destroying in the process 32,269 AP 
mines. While the number of AP mines discovered has steadily 
decreased since 2020 (when 8,740 AP mines were destroyed), 
Algeria continues to destroy very significant numbers in 
identified areas. In light of this, Algeria should now request a 
new Article 5 deadline to enable it to complete the work. This 
would be in line with the Convention’s agreed framework, 
which deems that in the event mined areas are discovered 
after the expiry of an Article 5 deadline, the relevant State 
should immediately inform all other States Parties of the 
discovery and undertake to destroy all AP mines as soon as 
possible. If, however, the affected State Party believes it will 
be unable to do so before the next Meeting of States Parties 
or Review Conference (whichever falls earlier), it should 
request an extended deadline. This process was accepted 
unanimously at the Twelfth Meeting  
of States Parties in 2012.2 
Cameroon and Mali have also not yet requested a 
new deadline from the other States Parties, despite 
acknowledging new use of AP mines of an improvised nature 
on their respective territories by non-State armed groups 
(NSAGs). They should do so at 22MSP in December 2025. 
Mali has, though, announced plans to submit an extension 
request by March 2026, which is a welcome development. 
Also positive, for the first time in fifteen years, Cameroon 
submitted an Article 7 report in 2025, covering 2023. It 
reiterated that no mined areas have been identified on its 
territory, but acknowledged that since 2014, improvised 
explosive devices (IEDs) used by NSAGs have caused 
casualties, particularly in its Far North region bordering 
Nigeria and its Anglophone regions, including several 
instances involving victim-activated devices that fall  
within the APMBC definition of an AP mine. 
More positively, in April 2025, Burkina Faso, also newly 
contaminated by the acts of NSAGs on its territory, submitted 
an extension request, allowing it to access greater support 
while respecting the principles of the Convention. Its request 
for a new Article 5 deadline of 31 December 2028 (its original 
ten-year deadline expired in 2009) was due to be considered 
at 22MSP.
With respect to the geographic spread, Asia (including 
the Middle East) is the most affected continent by number 
of countries, with 22 affected States. Following Oman’s 
completion of clearance at the end of 2024, among the 
States with AP mined areas in Asia, only eight are party to 
the Convention. Of Africa ’s 21 affected States, 18 are party 
to the APMBC, including Algeria which previously declared 
completion but which is finishing clearance of previously 
unknown mined areas. Only Egypt, Libya, and Morocco are 
not party to the APMBC. But in addition to those affected 
African States, “other area” Western Sahara is mine-affected. 
The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a member of the 
African Union, but is not recognised as a State by the UN 
Secretary-General in his capacity as depositary of more  
than 550 treaties, including the APMBC. 
1 These are territories not recognised as States by the Secretary-General of the United Nations (UN) in his capacity as treaty depositary for the APMBC.
2 Final Report of the Twelfth Meeting of States Parties, APMBC doc. APLC/MSP.12/2012/10, 21 January 2013, para. 28.

A question mark also remains over the situation in 
Mozambique, with evidence of the emplacement of 
victim-activated IEDs by Islamic State Mozambique 
Province (ISM) in the northern Cabo Delgado province. In 
the course of 2024, ISM began increasingly to rely on IEDs 
as a means of warfare. 3 While the group has largely sought 
to target military personnel, inevitably civilians have also 
been harmed. This continued to occur in 2025, with an IED 
injuring a civilian in Quiterajo on 19 May, and another injuring 
several civilians, including children, in Nangade on 23 May. 4 
In Nambija village in Macomia district, a civilian was killed 
by an IED in June 2025 – again the device seems to have 
been emplaced by ISM. 5 Mine Action Review will report on 
Mozambique in detail in next year’s report.
Benin, Côte d’Ivoire , and Togo have also seen incidents in 
recent years involving IEDs, 6 but publicly available data are 
scarce and it is unclear how many of the devices in question 
were victim-activated. In 2025, Côte d’Ivoire submitted its 
first Article 7 transparency report for ten years, covering 
calendar year 2024, in which it described the reporting form 
on mined areas as “not applicable”. Togo has not submitted 
an Article 7 report since 2004. Benin has not reported having 
identified or destroyed any improvised AP mines in its Article 
7 report covering 2008 to the end of 2023. 7
The extent of mined area in CAR  was unclear at the time of 
writing and Mine Action Review has removed it from the list 
of Article 5-affected States pending further information. In 
2025, CAR submitted an Article 7 report under the APMBC for 
the first time in 20 years, covering the period 2004–24. The 
report highlights a growing explosive ordnance threat since 
2020. While the problem of explosive ordnance contamination 
is certainly increasing, of the 44 explosive ordnance disposal 
(EOD) spot tasks undertaken in 2024 by the United Nations 
Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission (MINUSCA) 
and implementing partners for the UN Mine Action Service 
(UNMAS), 66 items of unexploded ordnance (UXO) but only 
a single improvised AP mine were destroyed. Nevertheless, 
UNMAS has acknowledged the possibility of significant 
under-reporting of incidents and victims while contamination 
is likely to exist that has not yet caused casualties. 8 
Accordingly, Mine Action Review recommends that CAR 
request a new interim deadline, giving the authorities time  
to assess the extent, if any, of its Article 5 obligations. 
In Europe, 10 States along with other area Kosovo are 
still mine-affected. These include six States Parties plus 
Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Russia. By far the heaviest 
contamination is in Ukraine , which has been massively 
contaminated with AP mines. While Ukraine has itself used 
AP mines—in serious violation of its obligations under the 
APMBC—Russia is easily the world’s biggest user, with 
many millions of AP mines remotely deployed and manually 
emplaced by its armed forces in the course of its aggression 
against Ukraine over the past three years. Azerbaijan is the 
second most affected European nation, with hundreds of 
square kilometres of mined area.
In the Americas , only four States remain affected by AP 
mines: States Parties Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru; and State 
not party Cuba. Increasing use of IEDs by the drug cartels in 
Mexico over recent years, some of which are victim activated 
and amount to AP mines, has been recorded. 9 Mexico’s Article 
7 report covering 2023 referenced an article in the Los 
Angeles Times on 9 March 2024 regarding the alleged use 
of IEDs by organized crime groups on Mexican territory, but 
affirmed that “the type of artifacts reported by the press, by 
their very nature, do not fall within the object or the scope 
of the APMBC.” In 2024, Mexico continued to experience 
a sharp increase in cartel-manufactured IEDs, mainly in 
Michoacán’s Tierra Caliente region, but with spillover into 
Jalisco and Guanajuato. Submission by Mexico of its Article 
7 report for 2024 was outstanding at the time of writing. 
While improvised anti-vehicle (AV) mines have certainly 
been used on occasion,10 available evidence does not enable 
a determination that Mexico has areas containing AP mines. 
Mine Action Review will continue to pay close attention  
to the situation as it evolves.

Every State should establish a national baseline of 
contamination as soon as security permits. This is the basis 
for effective planning towards completion. A number of States 
Parties to the APMBC still do not have a comprehensive 
baseline despite having joined the treaty more than two 
decades ago. Once a national baseline has been established, 
release through evidence-based non-technical and technical 
survey (NTS and TS) is then the critical focus. Such survey 
serves to confirm or discredit suspected contamination in 
specific areas, significantly reducing the size of hazardous 
areas from exaggerated estimates and enabling cancellation 
through NTS or reduction through TS in areas that have  
no mines.

evidence, which may differ from the view of the State Party 
in question.

7   Clearing the Mines 2025
ANTI-PERSONNEL MINES OF AN IMPROVISED NATURE
Significant numbers of AP mines of an improvised nature 
continued to be laid by NSAGs in 2024, including in Burkina 
Faso, Cameroon, Colombia, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, and Yemen. 
As the UN Secretary-General observed in July 2024, these 
devices are “a direct threat to civilians, humanitarian 
actors and security forces around the world”. 11 Improvised 
munitions are both captured by and prohibited under the 
APMBC whenever they are designed to be exploded by the 
presence, proximity, or contact of a person. The obligations to 
clear mined areas and report on progress under Article 5 and 
Article 7, respectively, apply to AP mines of an improvised 
nature just as they do to conventionally manufactured 
landmines.12 It does not matter under the APMBC how these 
weapons were produced or employed nor by whom they were 
laid – if they are located within the jurisdiction or control 
of a State Party, all of the Convention’s provisions apply. 
Technical guidance on how to dispose of IEDs, including AP 
mines of an improvised nature, has been incorporated into 
the International Mine Action Standards (IMAS). 13 Reporting 
guidelines that encompass improvised AP mines have also 
been adopted under the IMAS. 14 
Of course, improvised mines are not new and the mine 
action sector has addressed such contamination for 
decades. However, the prevalence of these improvised 
victim-activated munitions does appear to be increasing, 
posing a significant risk to civilians. As the States Parties to 
the APMBC highlighted in the Siem Reap-Angkor Declaration 
on a Mine-Free World 2024 concluded at the Fifth Review 
Conference in 2024: “We remain profoundly alarmed by 
the continued presence and use of anti-personnel mines, 
including those of an improvised nature, in new and 
protracted armed conflicts.” The States Parties undertook  
to “uphold, promote and strengthen the norms established by 
the Convention and remain determined to put an end to the 
suffering and casualties by antipersonnel mines, including 
those of an improvised nature.” 15 Reiterating a commitment 
made in the Oslo Action Plan, in the Siem Reap-Angkor Action 
Plan they declared that:
States Parties affected by anti-personnel mines of an 
improvised nature (improvised explosive devices (IEDs) 
which meet the definition of an anti-personnel mine) will 
apply all provisions and obligations under the Convention  
to such contamination including during survey and 
clearance in fulfilment of Article 5 and when reporting  
in fulfilment of Article 7.16
STATES THAT HAVE COMPLETED MINE CLEARANCE SINCE 1997
Since the adoption of the APMBC in 1997, clearance has been 
completed by 33 States  (see Table 3), 32 of which are party 
to the Convention, along with one other area (Taiwan). Nepal 
remains the only State not party to have completed mine 
clearance on its territory. Eleven of the States that completed 
clearance are from Africa; ten are from Europe; seven are 
from the Americas; and five are from Asia (including the 
Pacific and the Middle East). As mentioned above, Algeria  
has been removed from the list this year owing to its  
ongoing, planned clearance of mined areas.

MINE CLEARANCE IN 2024
Total global clearance of AP mined area in 2024 was 
175.39km2, which represents a drop of just over one quarter 
on the 2023 figure of 237.85km 2 (which was the highest 
annual clearance output ever recorded). 21 The decrease 
in global clearance was largely due to 38% decrease in 
clearance of mined area in State Party Cambodia , which fell 
by almost 50km2 (although it still undertook greater mine 
clearance than any other State by a significant margin). A 
33% global drop was recorded in the number of AP mines 
destroyed worldwide in the course of the year – down from 
195,416 in 202322 to 131,190 in 2024. 
Overall, of the 35 affected States Parties with AP mined area, 
15 cleared less mined area in 2024 compared to the previous 
year; 11 cleared the same amount or again did not conduct 
any mine clearance at all; and only 9 States Parties increased 
their annual clearance output in 2024. Some 93% of AP 
mined area cleared worldwide in 2024 occurred in States 
Parties to the APMBC . Four States Parties with the greatest 
annual clearance output—Afghanistan, Cambodia, Croatia, 
and Iraq—accounted for 81% of all mined area cleared 
globally in 2024. This is in stark contrast to affected States 
Parties Türkiye and South Sudan which each conducted less 
then 1km2 of AP mine clearance in 2024; to Algeria, Bosnia 
and Herzegovina, DR Congo, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Mauritania, 
Palestine, Peru, Senegal, Tajikistan, and Thailand each of 
which conducted less than 0.5km 2 of AP mine clearance; 
and Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Cyprus, Eritrea, 
Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Serbia, and Sudan which 
did not report any AP mine clearance at all for the year. 
Despite not releasing any mined area in 2024, Cameroon did, 
however, destroy 10 AP mines during EOD spot tasks; Chad 
destroyed 7 AP mines during route clearance; Guinea-Bissau 
released some mined area through TS and destroyed two 
AP mines; while Serbia released some mined area through 
TS. In contrast, Cyprus does not have effective control over 
remaining AP mined areas in the northern part of the island.
Of the non-signatories for which clearance data was 
available, Azerbaijan conducted the most clearance of AP 
mined area in 2024, followed by Syria and Israel. In Syria , 
the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 has enabled a 
shift to a countrywide approach to mine action coordination, 
with operators reporting improved access and cooperation. 
Clearance output increased in 2024 while survey output fell, 
but operators have been expanding survey and clearance 
capacity in 2025 to reach previously inaccessible areas. 
However, major challenges remain, including a surge in 
casualties, persistent funding shortfalls, the absence of a 
national contamination baseline, only nascent managerial 
capacity in the transitional government, and ongoing 
security risks. Syria is reportedly considering acceding 
to the Convention, which is to be strongly encouraged. In 
non-signatory Lebanon , mine clearance activities in the 
south along the Blue Line were suspended due to hostilities 
between Israel and Hezbollah that began on 8 October 2023 
and remained suspended throughout the whole of 2024. 
Disaggregated clearance output for AP mines for 2024 in 
several other non-signatories, such as Iran and Morrocco, 
has not been made public.

Clearing mined areas without finding any AP mines continued 
to occur in 2024. Among States Parties this concerned 
especially Angola, Colombia, Croatia, and Somalia. In Angola, 
this occurred over almost 1.6km 2 of mined area – half of 
total clearance for the year. Some of the tasks involved did, 
though, contain UXO. In Colombia, half of the area cleared in 
2024 contained no AP mines. In contrast, in Cambodia only  
six tasks covering 158,099m 2 were cleared without finding 
any mines in 2024, a big improvement on the 25 tasks 
covering more than 2km 2 that yielded no mines during  
the previous year.23
While the amount of area cleared in 2024 in Croatia increased 
over the previous year, the proportion of mines cleared 
per square metre equates to approximately one AP mine 
destroyed for every 30,000m 2 of cleared mined area – 
excluding items of UXO and AV mines destroyed. This is, 
however, a distinct improvement on the average of one AP 
mine per 52,000m 2 Croatia managed in 2023. The Croatian 
Mine Action Centre (CROMAC) reported that in 2024, 24 tasks 
totalling 13.19km2 were cleared with no AP mines found 
(although one AV mine and 277 items of UXO) were found. 24 
In 2024, The HALO Trust cleared ten AP mined areas in 
Somalia covering 0.65km 2 that proved to have no AP mines. 25 
In accordance with good practice in land release, mine 
clearance should only occur where firm evidence exists  
of actual contamination.
PROGRESS IN ARTICLE 5 IMPLEMENTATION IN MINE-AFFECTED 
STATES PARTIES
While all affected States and territories are obligated under 
international human rights law to clear AP mines as soon as 
possible on the basis of their customary law duty to protect 
life, States Parties to the APMBC have specific time-bound 
deadlines. Article 5 of the APMBC requires affected States 
Parties to complete mine clearance as soon as possible , 
but not later than ten years from becoming party to the 
Convention. If a State Party is unable to fulfil its Article 5 
obligations within the initial ten-year period, it may submit 
a request to a Meeting of the States Parties or a Review 
Conference for an extension of its deadline for a period of 
up to ten years at a time. In recent years, however, only one 
affected State—Ukraine—was granted an extension for the 
full ten years permissible and the overall trend has been for 
States Parties to request shorter extension periods, often  
for the amount of time they require to establish a baseline  
of mined area and elaborate a work plan for clearance. 
The extent of implementation of Article 5 clearance 
obligations varies widely between States Parties. Of the 
35 mine-affected States Parties as of 1 November 2025, 
only two States were believed to be on track to meet their 
respective treaty deadlines – Croatia , which is just on track 
to meet its deadline of 1 March 2026 and Peru , which is on 
track to meet its recently extended deadline of 31 December 
2029, having failed to meet its previous deadline of end of 
2024. Croatia should, however, submit an extension request 
for consideration at 22MSP in December 2025 if there is any 
doubt that it will meet the deadline. As noted above, Oman  
successfully met its original Article 5 deadline of 1 February 
2025 with time to spare. Hopes that Ecuador might also fulfil 
its Article 5 obligation by its end of 2025 deadline have been 
dashed and it has submitted a request to extend its deadline 
by two-years, for consideration at 22MSP. 
Progress to complete Article 5 implementation in both 
Cambodia and neighbouring Thailand  is now contingent 
on the two States reaching agreement to clear the border 
minefields, with the armed conflict between them in July 
2025 seemingly having put paid to any early resolution of this 
critical issue. Cambodia has denied Thai accusations that it 
had newly emplaced AP mines, and the allegations remained 
unverified at the time of writing. At the time of writing, 
Senegal risked heading for a determination that it is using 
AP mines. Its ongoing refusal, including in its 2025 Article 5 
deadline extension request, to declare whether mines remain 
around the Djirak or other military bases or provide detailed 
plans for clearing any remaining mined areas around military 
bases is not only an unjustified delay in clearance under 
Article 5 of the Convention, but also potentially constitutes 
prohibited use under Article 1.
The other 30 affected States Parties were either not on 
track to fulfil Article 5 in time or were in violation of their 
obligations under the Convention. Burkina Faso’s Article 5 
deadline expired on 1 March 2009, and its submission of an 
Article 5 deadline extension request in 2025 which is intended 
to enable it to generate a clearer understanding of the extent 
of new improvised AP mined area, is a welcome development. 
Cameroon and Mali should also each submit a request to 
extend their already expired respective Article 5 deadlines 
to address new contamination. As noted above, Mali has 
pledged to submit an extension request by March 2026 for 
consideration at 23MSP, which is a positive development. 
Mine Action Review recommends that Cameroon request 
a new deadline to conduct the necessary survey and more 
accurately assess the nature of the contamination, while 
continuing to strengthen national capacity, information 
management, and coordination to address the threat.

11   Clearing the Mines 2025
States in a position to provide assistance should support 
the three sub-Saharan States Parties that require a new 
Article 5 deadline (Burkina Faso, Cameroon, and Mali), 
to enable each to address AP mines of an improvised 
nature under the framework of the APMBC, as per their 
respective legal obligations. Each of these States will need to 
develop sustainable national capacities so they can collect, 
disaggregate, and record contamination data correctly, and 
accurately report AP mines of an improvised nature under 
the APMBC, as well as destroy them. 
Table 5 sets forth the Article 5 deadlines for all affected 
States Parties in alphabetical order, assessing progress 
in implementation of their international legal obligations. 
In 2025, 13 mine-affected States Parties were seeking an 
extension to their Article 5 deadline for consideration at 
22MSP: Angola, Burkina Faso, Cambodia, Colombia, DR 
Congo, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Senegal, South Sudan, 
Tajikistan, Türkiye, and Zimbabwe. As noted above, 
Argentina is also seeking a further three-year extension 
to its Article 5 deadline, but Mine Action Review does not 
consider Argentina to have an outstanding Article 5 obligation 
as clearance of mined areas in the Falkland Islands/Las 
Islas Malvinas has been completed. The three States Parties 
whose deadline has expired—and which must request  
a new Article 5 deadline in order to be in compliance  
with the Convention—are marked in bold in Table 5.

15   Clearing the Mines 2025
As of 1 November 2025, only Palestine and Sri Lanka were 
still within their respective original 10-year clearance 
deadline. All other States Parties had either been granted one 
(or more) extension periods or were currently in violation of 
the Convention. In 2024, the Fifth APMBC Review Conference 
granted further extensions to States Parties: Afghanistan, 
Chad, Eritrea, Cyprus, Guinea-Bissau, Niger, Peru, and Serbia. 
Eritrea is still in serious violation for its failure to resume 
survey or clearance of its mined areas. It was granted a 
three-year extension to its deadline to 31 December 2027 at 
the Fifth Review Conference in November 2024. In order to 
be in compliance with Article 5, however, Eritrea must also 
re-start survey and clearance of its mined areas.
As a matter of international law, Afghanistan  is represented 
by the Taliban government following its assumption of 
effective control of the territory of Afghanistan. The issue 
of recognition of the Taliban Government by the United 
Nations and individual States Parties is a separate matter 
from treaty application and implementation, just as it is 
under international humanitarian law. Since the change 
of regime, the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (IEA) is thus 
bound directly by the prohibitions on production, stockpiling, 
transfer, and use under Article 1 of the APMBC as well as by 
the duty to destroy or ensure the destruction of AP mines 
in Afghanistan under Article 5 and the duty to report on 
progress under Article 7. Mine Action Review hopes that the 
APMBC community can find a way to enable the Directorate 
of Mine Action Coordination (DMAC) to provide substantive 
updates to States Parties at future treaty meetings, on key 
provisions such as victim assistance and clearance, even  
if virtually.
PROGRAMME PERFORMANCE IN MINE-AFFECTED STATES PARTIES
To help affected States Parties and their partners focus their 
capacity development and technical assistance efforts on 
areas of need, and to improve the efficiency and effectiveness 
of survey and clearance programmes, a performance scoring 
system is used by Mine Action Review. For their survey and 
clearance work in 2024, each of the affected States Parties 
was scored on the basis of the following eight criteria: 
 ■ Understanding of AP mine contamination, 
 ■ National ownership and programme management,
 ■ Gender and diversity, 
 ■ Environmental policies and action,
 ■ Information management and reporting, 
 ■ Planning and tasking, 
 ■ Land release system, and 
 ■ Land release outputs and Article 5 compliance.
The text box below outlines the eight programme 
performance criteria and key factors affecting scoring  
in detail.
Mine Action Review Criteria to Assess National Programme Performance of States Parties to the APMBC 
Criterion Key Factors Affecting Scoring
UNDERSTANDING  
OF AP MINE CONTAMINATION
(20% of overall score)
 ■ Has a national baseline of AP mine contamination been established  
and is it up to date and accurate?
 ■ If no national baseline, or only a partial or inaccurate baseline, exists,  
is survey and/or re-survey being conducted or is it planned?
 ■ Are mined areas disaggregated from areas with other types of explosive 
ordnance (e.g. other explosive remnants of war (ERW) such as submunitions)?
 ■ Is contamination classified into suspected hazardous areas (SHAs)  
and confirmed hazardous areas (CHAs), based on whether there  
is indirect or direct evidence of mines, respectively? 
 ■ Is there a high ratio of CHAs to SHAs? 
NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND 
PROGRAMME MANAGEMENT
(10% of overall score)
 ■ Is there a national entity, such as a national mine action authority,  
overseeing mine action? 
 ■ Is there a national mine action centre coordinating operations? 
 ■ Are the roles and responsibilities in mine action clear and coherent  
within the national programme? 
 ■ Is the mine action centre adequately staffed and skilled? 
 ■ Are clearance operators involved in key decision-making processes?
 ■ Does national legislation, or other suitable administrative measures,  
effectively underpin the mine action programme?
 ■ Have the authorities created an enabling environment for mine action? 
 ■ Has the government facilitated the receipt and efficient use of international 
assistance?
 ■ Is there political will for timely and efficient implementation of Article 5  
of the APMBC?
 ■ Does the affected State contribute national resources to support the cost  
of the mine action centre and/or survey and clearance of mined areas?
 ■ Does the affected State have a resource mobilisation strategy in place  
for Article 5 implementation?

Criterion Key Factors Affecting Scoring
GENDER AND DIVERSITY
(10% of overall score)
 ■ Does the national mine action programme have a gender policy and 
implementation plan? Do the main mine action operators have one? 
 ■ Is gender mainstreamed in the national mine action strategy and national  
mine action standards? 
 ■ Are women and children in communities affected by mined areas consulted 
during survey and community liaison activities?
 ■ Are survey and community liaison teams inclusive and gender balanced, to 
facilitate access and participation by all groups, including women and children?
 ■ Are the needs of women and children in communities affected by mined  
areas considered in the prioritisation, planning, and tasking of survey

 ■ Are ethnic or minority groups in communities affected by mined areas 
consulted during survey and community liaison activities?
 ■ Do survey, clearance, and community liaison teams include representatives 
from different ethnic or minority groups, to facilitate access and participation 
by all groups?
 ■ Are the needs of ethnic or minority groups in communities affected by mined 
areas considered in the prioritisation, planning, and tasking of survey and 
clearance activities?
 ■ Is relevant mine action data disaggregated by gender and age? 
 ■ Is there equal access to employment for qualified women and men in survey 
and clearance teams, including for managerial level/supervisory positions? 
ENVIRONMENTAL 
POLICIES AND ACTION
(10% of overall score)
 ■ Does the national mine action programme have an environmental  
management policy? 
 ■ Does the affected State have a national mine action standard (NMAS)  
on environmental management and climate change in mine action?  
If yes, is it in line with IMAS 07.13?
 ■ Are environmental assessments conducted to support informed 
decision-making on the planning and delivery of survey and clearance tasks?
 ■ Where required, are measures implemented to prevent or minimise 
environmental harm, including to reduce greenhouse gas emissions,  
during demining operations, at demining camps, at mine action centres,  
and during travel?
 ■ When planning and prioritising survey and clearance tasks, is the affected 
State taking into account climate-related or extreme weather risks (such  
as increased risk of flooding that may cause operations to be stood down  
or potentially displace mines or even displace people into contaminated areas)? 
INFORMATION MANAGEMENT  
AND REPORTING
(10% of overall score)
 ■ Is there a national information management system in place (e.g. IMSMA),  
and is the data accurate and reliable?
 ■ Are data collection forms consistent and do they enable collection  
of the necessary data?
 ■ Is data in the information management system disaggregated by type  
of contamination and method of land release? 
 ■ Is the data in the information management system accessible to all operators?
 ■ Are ongoing efforts being made to ensure or improve the quality of data  
in the mine action database?
 ■ Does the affected State Party submit accurate and timely annual Article 7 
reports on Article 5 progress?
 ■ Are Article 5 deadline extension requests of a high-quality and submitted  
in a timely manner?
 ■ Is the survey and clearance data reported by the affected State Party  
(e.g. in Article 7 reporting) accurate and disaggregated by type of 
contamination (i.e. mines from ERW) and method of land release?
 ■ Does the affected State Party report on progress in Article 5 implementation 
at the Meetings of States Parties and Intersessional Meetings and is reporting 
accurate and consistent between reporting periods?

PLANNING AND TASKING
(10% of overall score)
 ■ Is there a national mine action strategy in place and does it include realistic

 ■ Is there a realistic annual work plan in place for land release?

(10% of overall score)
 ■ Does the affected State have national mine action standards in place  
for land release? 
 ■ Do the standards enable or impede efficient evidence-based survey  
and clearance?
 ■ Are national standards reflected in standard operating procedures (SOPs)?
 ■ Are standards and SOPs periodically reviewed against IMAS and international

 ■ Are areas being cleared that prove to have no mine contamination?
 ■ Where relevant, is there national survey and clearance capacity in place to 
address mines discovered after the release of mined areas or post completion?
 ■ Is there an appropriate range of demining assets (manual, mechanical,  
and animal detection systems) integrated into land release operations?
 ■ Is there an effective quality management system in place for survey  
and clearance operations?
 ■ Where an accident has occurred within a mine action programme, was there  
an effective investigation? Were lessons learned shared between operators? 
LAND RELEASE OUTPUTS AND 
ARTICLE 5 COMPLIANCE
(20% of overall score)
 ■ Is the affected State seeking to clear all AP mines from territory under  
its jurisdiction or control, including along national borders, in and around 
military installations, and in hard to access areas?
 ■ Have national mine action authorities set a target date for the completion  
of mine clearance and is this within the State Party’s Article 5 deadline? 
 ■ Is the target date for completion ambitious, yet realistic, based on  
existing capacity?
 ■ What were the outputs of survey and clearance of mined area in 2024,  
and were they greater or lesser than the previous year and why?
 ■ Are survey and clearance outputs in line with plans and Article 5 obligations?
 ■ Is the affected State on track to meet the target completion date and/or  
Article 5 deadline?
In the scoring, given their relative importance, double 
weighting is accorded to two criteria: Understanding of AP 
mine contamination; and Land release outputs and Article 5 
compliance. An average is then calculated that determines 
the overall score. A score of 8 or more is ranked Very Good. 
A score of 7.0–7.9 is ranked Good. A score of 5.0–6.9 is ranked 
Average. A score of 4.0–4.9 is ranked Poor. A score of less 
than 4 is ranked Very Poor. 
The results of the scoring for 2024 are summarised in Table 
6. The country-specific assessments of the eight criteria, 
which should be viewed alongside the recommendations 
for action in the country reports, are intended as an 
implementation tool to assist States Parties to identify and 
overcome challenges and fulfil their Article 5 obligations as 
efficiently as possible.
For 2024, no mine action programme was rated “Very Good”. 
This was also the case for 2023. Zimbabwe  remained the top 
scoring State Party . Angola, Cambodia, Oman, and Thailand 
were also rated Good. Ethiopia and Somalia moved up to 
Average from Poor, joining Afghanistan, Colombia, Croatia, 
DR Congo, Ecuador, Guinea-Bissau, Iraq, Mauritania, Peru, 
Serbia, South Sudan, Sri Lanka, Sudan, Tajikistan, and 
Türkiye. Bosnia and Herzegovina dropped to a Poor rating, 
joining Burkina Faso (ranked for the first time this year), 
Chad, Senegal, Ukraine, and Yemen. Despite remaining 
as Very Poor, Nigeria’s performance in 2024 increased, 
compared to the previous year, indicating a positive trajectory 
as it establishes its national mine action programme. Eritrea 
and Niger also continued to be ranked as Very Poor for 2024, 
joined by Cameroon (ranked for the first time).

26 ‘The States Parties have defined national ownership as entailing the following: ‘maintaining interest at a high level in fulfilling Convention obligations and

Convention; articulating the measures its state entities undertake to implement relevant aspects of the Convention in the most inclusive, efficient and expedient 
manner possible and plans to overcome any challenges that need to be addressed; and, making a regular significant national financial commitment to the state’s

27 Siem Reap–Angkor Action Plan 2025–2029, paragraph 5.
28 Action 5, Siem Reap-Angkor Action Plan 2025–2029.
THE SIEM REAP-ANGKOR ACTION PLAN
The Fifth Review Conference of the APMBC took place in Siem 
Reap, Cambodia on 25–29 November 2024. Under Cambodia’s 
presidency of the Review Conference and in collaboration 
with States Parties, mine action NGOs, and other expert 
organisations, the five-year Siem Reap-Angkor Action Plan 
(SRAAP) was elaborated, building on the Oslo Action Plan 
(OAP) which was adopted in 2019.
The SRAAP is a blueprint for implementation of the 
Convention, supporting States Parties and their implementing 
partners get to completion in the best way possible – 
efficiently, effectively, safely, and inclusively. The Action 
Plan has actions with measurable indicators. A baseline of 
the current status of implementation will be established, 
against which progress will be measured year-on-year 
up to the next Review Conference in 2029. It is essential 
for national authorities to have the systems in place to 
support implementation of the Treaty and of the SRAAP. 
This means ensuring that the obligations in Article 5 and the 
guidance provided by the SRAAP are integrated into national 
strategies, annual work plans, information management 
systems, and national mine action standards. National 
ownership, the subject of the first Action, is critical to 
successful Article 5 implementation. 26
Monitoring the Siem Reap-Angkor Action Plan
Members of the Coordinating Committee, under the auspices 
of the APMBC Presidency, will be responsible for establishing 
a baseline value for the SRAAP and measuring progress 
in implementing the APMBC within their mandates, with 
the support of the Implementation Support Unit (ISU). The 
information submitted in the States Parties’ annual Article 7 
will serve as the main source of data to assess progress. 27
In addition to the official APMBC monitoring of the SRAAP, 
Mine Action Review is also providing civil society monitoring 
and analysis of the implementation of the SRAAP actions 
relating to survey and clearance. This is based on our 
broader research, which includes not only official treaty 
reporting (Article 7 reports and official government 
statements and updates under the Convention), but also 
liaison with national mine action authorities and mine action 
centres, clearance operators, UNMAS, the UN Development 
Programme (UNDP), the Organization for Security and 
Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), and the Geneva International 
Centre for Humanitarian Demining (GICHD).
This year’s baseline results of Mine Action Review’s 2025 
monitoring of survey- and clearance-related indicators  
in the SRAAP can be found on the Mine Action Review 
website. Mine Action Review welcomes feedback from 
States Parties and other stakeholders on the results of the 
assessment. Please send an email with any feedback or 
additional information for Mine Action Review’s consideration  
to MineActionReview@npaid.org.
As the 2025 baseline of current progress illustrates, States 
Parties have not yet fully implemented the actions and 
indicators applicable to them. But the hope is that through 
the efforts of national authorities, with the support of 
implementing partners, they can identify where there are 
gaps and make progress in addressing them, which will then 
be reflected in progress in the indicators each year between 
now and the Sixth Review Conference in 2029.
GENDER AND DIVERSITY
Since Norway’s leadership on gender and diversity during 
its Presidency of the Fourth Review Conference in 2019, the 
sector has seen significant progress in the mainstreaming of 
gender and diversity considerations in treaty implementation. 
In the Siem Reap-Angkor Declaration on a Mine-Free 
World 2024, adopted at the Fifth Review Conference, 
States Parties built on a similar commitment in the Oslo 
Declaration and declared: “We recognise the importance of 
our implementation efforts ensuring consideration for the 
different needs and vulnerabilities of girls, women, boys, and 
men, including mine victims, in mine-affected communities, 
as well as other factors such as disability, ethnicity, and 
different socio-economic groups. By ensuring an inclusive 
approach, including removing barriers to full, equal, and 
gender-balanced participation in mine action and Convention 
meetings, we aim to protect all people from the negative 
consequences of anti-personnel mines”. 28 Building on the Oslo 
Action Plan, gender and diversity were similarly embedded 
throughout the Siem Reap-Angkor Action Plan 2024–2029.
With respect to Mine Action Review’s assessment of the 
performance of States Parties against the “gender and 
diversity” criterion, the performance of five of 32 States 
Parties assessed improved in 2024 compared to the previous 
year, the performance of 26 States Parties remained 
constant, and one State Party (Afghanistan) declined in 
performance. Mine Action Review again scored Cambodia 
as the highest ranking State Party for its performance 
on gender and diversity in 2024. Cambodia, together with 
Colombia, remained the only two States Parties to achieve a 
rating of “Very Good”. Both provide good examples to other 
mine-affected States Parties on what efforts can be taken to 
mainstream gender and diversity. While five States Parties 
were rated Good, fifteen were judged to be Average, five  
were Poor, and five were Very Poor, demonstrating there  
is still significant room for improvement in most affected 
States Parties.

A selection of both positive and disappointing examples from 
Mine Action Review’s research on affected States Parties are 
included below, but for additional information please see the 
Gender and Diversity section of the individual Clearing the 
Mines 2025 country reports. The country reports include the 
number and percentage of women working at national mine 
action centres and clearance operators, including those in 
managerial/supervisory roles and operational positions.
Cambodia has again led the way in mainstreaming gender 
in its mine action programme. The Cambodian Mine Action 
and Victim Assistance Authority (CMAA) is implementing 
a Gender Mainstreaming in Mine Action Plan (GMMAP) in 
line with the objectives of the National Mine Action Strategy 
2018–2025. In 2024, it adopted a national standard on 
mainstreaming gender and diversity in mine action, the first 
programme to do so, establishing mandatory requirements 
for operators and reinforcing a commitment to inclusion. 
Among operators, The HALO Trust was again a leading  
light, with 41% of its 1,190 staff women, and 45% of its  
978 operational positions filled by women.
In Colombia, the Knowledge Management Platform, 
established in 2024, includes a technical group dedicated 
to cross-cutting approaches including gender and ethnicity, 
with the goal of promoting practical, inclusive approaches 
that address inequalities and reflect the diverse identities of 
affected populations. While the proportion of women in the 
National Army’s Humanitarian Demining Brigade (BRDEH) 
and in the BDIAN (previously known as the Marine Corps 
Explosives and Demining Association, AEDIM) disappointingly 
remained extremely low, Colombia continued to have 
one of the highest rates of women’s participation in the 
global mine action sector among civilian operators. The 
five civilian operators reported employing a total of 416 
women out of 1,038 staff members in 2024 – amounting 
to some 40%. A majority (52%) of the employees of the 
coordinating OCCP-AICMA Group are women. Humanity & 
Inclusion (HI) has a majority (18 of 35) of its managerial/
supervisory positions filled by women. In addition, all civilian 
demining operators have gender focal points, although their 
structure and responsibilities vary. What is more, in 2024, 
all operators reported implementing initiatives to strengthen 
the integration of gender and diversity in their programmes. 29 
National operator the Colombian Campaign to Ban Landmines 
(CCCM) organised a workshop for focal points from 
Afro-descendant and Indigenous communities, a community 
garden project linking gender-based violence prevention 
with land care, a cultural diversity bazaar in Putumayo, and a 
leadership meeting for women affected by armed conflict. 
In Angola in 2024, Norwegian People’s Aid (NPA) supported 
the national mine action agency (ANAM) to develop its first 
national mine action gender equality and diversity policy. 
NPA was the only operator to increase the proportion of 
women employed in 2024, although it still lags far behind 
HALO, which has nearly achieved gender parity overall with 
41% of its more than 1,500 staff being female. Women are, 
however, still under-represented in HALO’s managerial and 
supervisory positions. In 2024, an EOD Level 2 course was 
completed by 11 participants, of whom five were female staff 
from Mines Advisory Group (MAG).
In 2025, Cameroon  was serving as the gender focal point 
of the APMBC Committee on Cooperation and Assistance, 
but domestically, it has still to detail how gender and 
diversity are considered in its defence sector, and its Article 
7 reporting data were not disaggregated. That said, the 
Cameroonian Army Engineering Corps includes women 
among its deminers, serving in various units, including  
those tasked with EOD. 
Ukraine also appears to be making some progress in 
promoting gender, diversity, and inclusion. Its national mine 
action strategy published in 2024 contains nine measures 
intended to ensure equality and inclusion and specifies 
professional involvement in mine action of women, veterans, 
persons with disabilities, and victims of explosive ordnance 
as a State priority. A national working group on gender in 
mine action is up and running, and an assessment on gender 
and diversity in mine action was conducted for the first time 
in 2024.
In Iraq, despite increased political sensitivity around gender 
issues, the national mine action strategy continues to 
support diversity while operators have adapted recruitment 
and employment conditions to meet resistance posed by 
conservative social attitudes to women’s employment in the 
sector. National NGO Shahreteah Humanitarian Organisation 
(SHO) led the sector, with women comprising nearly 40% 
of its staff. HALO provided childcare support for all female 
staff with children, helping to ensure they were able to stay 
in full-time employment.30 MAG increased the number of 
women in leadership positions and for the first time had 
three national women staff in its senior management team. It 
introduced new recruitment standard operating procedures 
(SOPs) in 2024 to facilitate entry of under-represented 
groups and address religious diversity by accommodating 
observances of Christian, Yazidi, and Muslim staff as well as 
providing separate rest areas for men and women. 31
In Tajikistan, while the mine action programme has a gender 
strategy few women are employed in the sector and none 
work in the Ministry of Defence Humanitarian Demining 
Company (MoD HDC), the largest operator. A gender and 
diversity working group did reconvene in 2024, having not 
met since 2022. In Bosnia and Herzegovina ’s mine action 
centre (BHMAC) only 23% of staff are women. But the 
figures are even worse in MAG and NPA, with 13% and 12%, 
respectively. Moreover, among operational staff, the figures 
drop further – to 8% and 7%, respectively.
In Afghanistan , implementing partners, with DMAC’s support, 
have been able to keep some women in office and field roles 
(in risk education and community liaison) but draconian 
Taliban restrictions on women in public life 32 continue to 
undercut meaningful Mine Action Programme of Afghanistan 
(MAPA) gender mainstreaming, and conditions for deploying 
female staff vary regionally. Funding cuts, which have 
impacted national implementing partners particularly 
severely, are driving down female employment in mine  
action even further.

ENVIRONMENTAL POLICIES AND ACTION IN AFFECTED  
STATES PARTIES 
In the Siem Reap-Angkor Declaration on a Mine-Free 
World 2024, States Parties declared that: “We recognise 
that climate change and environmental degradation can 
exacerbate challenges in affected communities and commit 
to adopting environmentally-sound practices and take 
climate considerations into account in the prioritisation 
and implementation of the Convention .”33 Climate and the 
environmental considerations have also been incorporated 
throughout the Siem Reap-Angkor Action Plan 2025–2029,  
an element largely absent in the Oslo Action Plan.
Every mine action programme should systematically assess, 
and where possible prevent or mitigate, possible adverse 
environmental impacts of their activities. There is also 
significant potential for mine action to support efforts to 
stem, but also adapt to, the effects of climate change  
and to proactively protect the environment.
International Mine Action Standard (IMAS) 07.13 on 
environmental management in mine action, first published 
in 2017, was revised and adopted in 2024 and is now entitled 
“Environmental management and climate change in mine 
action”.34 It provides a valuable framework for action by the 
mine action sector. In addition, a Technical Note on Mine 
Action (TNMA) 7.13/01,35 published in January 2025, provides 
further guidance and a list of practical measures to be used 
by national mine action authorities, mine action centres, and 
mine action organisations to support the implementation 
of IMAS 07.13. All affected States should elaborate and 
implement a national mine action standard (NMAS)  
on environmental management and climate change,  
in line with IMAS 07.13 Second Edition.
A new Mine Action Review policy brief, Environmental 
Protection in Mine Action: An Overview of Good Policy 
and Practice, published in November 2024, is available 
for download on the Mine Action Review website. The 
policy brief is based on the premise that every NMAA and 
mine action operator should be embedding environmental 
and climate-change considerations at each stage of the 
mine action process – from planning to operations to 
post-clearance activities. The aim is to inspire and equip all 
mine action stakeholders to elaborate, adopt, and implement 
policies and practices that minimise environmental harm; 
contribute to climate resilience; and maximise the positive 
benefits of land release on both the human beneficiaries and 
the planet we all share. The policy brief serves three main 
purposes: guiding policy development; showcasing good 
practice; and advocating for greater donor engagement.
In addition, we encourage affected States and their 
implementing partners to make use of environmental 
assessment tools, such as the Green Field Tool (GFT) —  
an environmental assessment and screening tool developed 
by NPA and the Conflict and Environment Observatory 
(CEOBS). It is designed to support environmentally 
responsible planning and implementation of mine action 
activities, including the consideration of the potential risks 
from the impact of climate change on mine action activities 
and affected communities. The tool and its supporting 
guidance are available on the resources page of the 
environmentinmineaction.org  website. Environmental 
assessments should ideally be conducted as early as possible 
in the planning process, including during programme design, 
community engagement, and NTS which has the added 
benefit of saving workdays and reducing costs.
Several mine-affected States and other areas, such as 
Afghanistan, Armenia, Cambodia, Georgia, Israel, Kosovo, 
the Lao People’s Democratic Republic (Lao PDR), Lebanon, 
Senegal, South Sudan, Tajikistan, Thailand, Türkiye, 
Yemen, and Zimbabwe, now have a dedicated NMAS on 
the environment, and others (DR Congo and Ukraine) 
incorporate the environment, but currently lack a dedicated 
environmental standard. All affected States should elaborate 
and implement an NMAS on environmental management and 
climate change, in line with IMAS 07.13. Clearance operators 
also have environmental policies and management systems 
in place at their headquarters and sometimes also in country 
programmes, although the comprehensiveness of these 
varies across organisations. Some international clearance 
operators now have dedicated personnel working on the 
environment at head office and country level. 
Last year, Mine Action Review introduced a new criterion on 
“Environmental policies and action” to the framework used 
to annually assess the performance of national mine action 
programmes in APMBC States Parties. There continued to be 
significant advances in protecting the environment in certain 
States Parties in 2024. In some instances, the achievements 
were regulatory in nature, while in others, practical progress 
in the field was documented. 
Examples of some of the latest developments are included 
below, but for additional information please see the 
Environmental Policies and Action section of the country 
reports for each State Party. As they had done a year earlier, 
Croatia, South Sudan, Tajikistan, and Zimbabwe again 
achieved the highest scores for their performance in 2024 
with respect to Mine Action Review’s assessment criterion 
of “Environmental policies and action”, joined by Peru which 
was previously assessed as average for its performance  
in 2023.
In Angola in 2024, APOPO increased its efforts to reduce 
generator reliance and vegetation cutting during operations 
and has been undertaking an analysis of greenhouse gas 
emissions through standardised reporting protocols. 
The HALO Trust has recruited an Environment Project 
Coordinator and commissioned the conduct of environmental 
impact assessments (EIAs) and an Environmental 
Management Plan for implementation in the second 
half of 2025. HALO also delivered large-scale forestry 
inventories for the US Forestry Service, conducted surveys

In Cambodia, under the national standard, operators are 
required to take account of erosion or soil degradation; 
possible pollution of air, water, or soil; and damage to 
infrastructure, wildlife, and vegetation, while also dealing 
with litter, debris, and other waste as well as damage to 
heritage sites or objects. The CMAA held a two-day workshop 
with operators in 2024 on environmental management. 
NPA also rolled out its “Green Field Tool” during the year, 
requiring environmental impact assessments of all survey 
and clearance tasks.
Iraq ranks among the five most vulnerable nations to effects 
of climate change, including drought, water scarcity, flash 
floods, frequent sand and dust storms, and extreme heat, all 
of which pose a growing operational challenge. While Iraq 
has yet to elaborate a policy or national mine action standard 
on environmental management in mine action, the GICHD and 
the Ministry of Environment conducted a workshop in 2024 to 
develop approaches to environmental management in mine 
action. Demining organisations mostly apply their own SOPs 
for managing the environment and minimising harm from 
operations. NPA appointed an Environmental Advisor for  
the Iraq programme in August 2024.
Peru is seeking to minimise the environmental impact of 
demining in the Cordillera del Cóndor, aligning operations 
with the Master Plan for the Ichigkat National Park (2019–23). 
In 2024, the programme appointed an environmental 
focal point within CONTRAMINAS and began reviewing 
national mine action standards to align with IMAS 07.13 on 
environmental management. Its 2024 Article 5 deadline 
extension request underscored the growing impact of climate 
change, with heavy rains frequently delaying operations and 
affecting the accuracy of CHA locations, prompting use  
of a 600-metre buffer zone during land release.
In Sri Lanka , which does not have an NMAS on environmental 
protection, operators and the National Mine Action 
Centre nonetheless consider seasonal weather changes 
and associated climate-related risks when planning and 
prioritising survey and clearance. 36 For instance, The HALO 
Trust prioritises areas prone to flooding or waterlogging 
to minimise disruption and reduce the risk of landmine 
movement.37 Such areas are scheduled for clearance outside 
the rainy season wherever possible, guided by historical 
weather patterns and local knowledge. Clearance of 
flood-prone sites is generally advanced into the drier months 
when ground conditions allow safer and more efficient 
operations. If ground saturation occurs unexpectedly, work 
may be paused until conditions improve. MAG reported 
that the impact of climate change on seasonal rains in Sri 
Lanka has become increasingly evident, and in both January 
2024 and January 2025, heavy rainfall caused near-total 
suspension of operations. 38
In Tajikistan, a mine action working group on the 
Climate Change and Environment has been established, 
which includes participation from NPA, FSD, OSCE, the 
Humanitarian Demining Company of the Ministry of Defence, 
Union of Sappers of Tajikistan, and the Red Crescent 
Society of Tajikistan. A representative of the Committee for 
Environmental Protection under the Government of Tajikistan 
will also participate in this Working group so that the planned 
activities are coordinated and agreed. The working group 
is intended to provide technical expertise, strategic advice, 
and coordination on climate change and environment-related 
issues. The first of planned bi-annual meetings was held in 
June 2024 to identify possible steps on how the mine action 
community can contribute to the environment protection. 39 
Thailand has had an NMAS on environmental management 
in place since 2010 but which is in need of revision and 
updating. In 2024, NPA piloted environmentally responsible 
planning of clearance operations in Phanom Dong Rak 
Wildlife Sanctuary and took new measures to manage waste 
in its head office and field operations and reduce vehicle 
emissions. NPA also held a seminar on climate awareness for 
NPA and Thai Mine Action Centre (TMAC) staff and co-hosted 
a regional workshop on tackling the environmental impact  
of explosive remnants of war.
In Zimbabwe, operators are taking a range of steps to reduce 
their carbon emissions. HALO field camps have been run on 
solar power since 2016. HALO also uses electric strimmers to 
clear vegetation. NPA extended solar panel installation to the 
remaining two of its three field camps in 2024. MAG continued 
to use solar power for field activities and is collecting 
data within its Zimbabwe programme for a global Carbon 
Accounting Project, which should offer further country-level 
advice on minimising its local environmental impact. In line 
with its global initiative, APOPO had a carbon sequestration 
plan for its Zimbabwe programme, which included emissions 
reduction and a primary goal to plant and monitor more  
than 110,000 trees.
OUTLOOK
Huge progress has been made in implementing the obligations set out in Article 5 of the APMBC in States Parties  
and in improving the practices of the mine action sector more broadly. But given the potent headwinds confronting  
the implementation of the Convention, the decisions and actions of States Parties at the Twenty-Second Meeting of States  
Parties will be critical in determining its future for years to come. Who will stand up and be counted in 2025?

CLEARING

KEY DATA
KEY DEVELOPMENTS
Afghanistan requested a five-year extension of its Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention (APMBC) Article 5 deadline in 2024, 
which was granted at the Fifth Review Conference in Siem Reap in November. Lower donor financial support caused the Mine 
Action Programme of Afghanistan (MAPA) to lose one third of its personnel and cut United Nations (UN) capacity to support 
coordination and quality management. Implementing partners achieved a sharp rise in land cancelled through non-technical 
survey (NTS) and a slight increase in clearance of areas contaminated by improvised mines but clearance of “legacy” 
anti-personnel (AP) mines fell sharply. 
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ACTION 
 ■ The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (IEA) should increase and expedite delivery of national funding for the  
mine action sector, including by integrating demining into projects undertaken by government ministries.
 ■ The IEA and the Directorate of Mine Action Coordination (DMAC) should enhance the participation of women  
in mine action.
 ■ International donors should put funding for the critical support provided by the Mine Action Technical Cell (MATC) 
on a stable, long-term basis.

UNDERSTANDING OF AP MINE CONTAMINATION
Afghanistan estimated conventional and improvised AP mined area as covering 182km 2 at the end of 2024 (see Table 1), 3% 
more than a year earlier, reflecting increased knowledge of the improvised mine threat. The level of contamination by “legacy” 
conventional AP mines was 8% lower than at the end of 2023. 1 Operators identified 2.7km 2 of previously unrecorded mined area 
in 2024, a fraction of what they found in 2023 (49km 2), and mostly located in the eastern half of the country. 2

Legacy mine contamination, dating from before 2001, affects 30 (90%) of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces but has fallen by  
one third – from 152km2 at the end of 2020 to 103km 2 four years later. The mines, which are mainly concentrated in north 
eastern and central provinces, notably Baghlan, Badakshan, Kabul and Parwan (see Table 2), result from the decade-long 
war of resistance that followed the Soviet invasion of 1979, the 1992–96 internal armed conflict, and the 1996−2001 fighting 
between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance. Much of what remains after two decades of clearance is located in remote and 
mountainous areas and as a result receives a lower clearance priority than other forms of explosive ordnance, which cause a 
higher number of casualties.

province which, together with neighbouring Helmand and the south-eastern province of Ghazni, account for 61% of the total 
estimated contamination. 6
